messages.subject: MC samples from generic density with unkown normalization, using slice sampler
parts:
Dear Nimble devs & users,

I'm an excited newbie. Could you help me with two simple questions? I've been checking the examples and manual but haven't managed to find answers to them yet.

1. Suppose I want to draw samples from a generic density with unknown normalization constant. Say,

P(x) = exp(-x^2) * abs(ln(x))/Z

with Z unknown (of course here it could be calculated numerically, but this may not be possible in higher dimensions). How do build a Nimble model to sample from it via MCMC?

I tried first defining the density 'dmyexplog' as a nimbleFunction, but when I run the MC sampler I get the warning "user-defined distribution dmyexplog provided without random generation function". Of course I cannot provide a random generator because that's my objective. Then I tried defining the nimbleCode directly as

nimbleCode({
x <- exp(-x^2) * abs(log(x))
})

but this also gives an error.


2. How do I assign a specific sampler, say AF_slice, for the MCMC, say for the variable 'x'? After setting up a model I tried with

conf <- configureMCMC(model)
conf$removeSamplers('x')
conf$addSampler(target='x', type='AF_slice')

but at compilation time my choice seems to disappear.

Thank you very much for your help!
Cheers,
Luca

messages.subject: Re: MC samples from generic density with unkown normalization, using slice sampler
parts:
Dear all,

I've been exploring nimble some more, and it seems that I can define and use an unnormalized distribution, as long as I specify a MC sampler for it.

Here is an example skeleton code as an answer to both of my previous questions. It samples from a bivariate normal, assuming that we don't know its normalization constant, using the adaptive slice sampler.

I'd appreciate if you pointed out errors or more efficient ways to do this:

library('nimble')
dmymnorm <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(x=double(1), means=double(1), log=integer(0, default=0)){
returnType(double(0))
logprob <- -sum((x-means)^2)/2 # not normalized
if(log) return(logprob)
else return(exp(logprob))
})
assign('dmymnorm', dmymnorm, envir = .GlobalEnv)
mycode <- nimbleCode({
X[1:2] ~ dmymnorm(means=means[1:2])
})
myconstants <- list(means=0:1)
myinits <- list(X=0:1)
mymodel <- nimbleModel(code=mycode, name='mymodel', constants=myconstants, inits=myinits, data=list())
Cmymodel <- compileNimble(mymodel, resetFunctions = TRUE)
myconf <- configureMCMC(Cmymodel, nodes=NULL)
myconf$addSampler(target='X', type='AF_slice', control=list())
mymcmc <- buildMCMC(myconf)
Cmymcmc <- compileNimble(mymcmc, resetFunctions = TRUE)
myMCsamples <- runMCMC(Cmymcmc)
hist(myMCsamples[,1])


Cheers,
Luca

parts:
Dear Luca,

Thanks for posting your original question and also follow-up before anyone replied to the original!

It looks like you got it working.  I'll just add a few comments in case they are helpful.

The warning you saw is only that, a warning, not an error.  I think it would have also said that a proxy (do-nothing) "r" function will be automatically created, and if no algorithm needs to call the "r" function, it is no problem that you didn't provide one.

I am not sure why adding the AF_slice sampler did not seem to work at first.  It might have been because that is a block sampler and in your first code it looks like you were assigning it to a scalar target (a single node).  In your second example you have a multivariate node, so that makes more sense.  I just checked the source code and I see there is an error-trap for assigning AF_slice to a scalar target, so I will file an issue for us to check on why that might have failed to correctly trap the error, if that was indeed the situation.

If you want to debug dmymnorm, for example, to see what values it is being called with from the model, you can do so in uncompiled execution.  E.g. "debug(dmymnorm)" and then "mymcmc$run(10)"

Good luck and thanks for posting the question.

-Perry

Dear Perry and everyone,

Thank you for the feedback, information, and suggestions! The problem with the AF_slice sampler was probably caused by my misuse of "addSampler()".

I'm still unsure on how to use a non-normalize log-probability in Nimble. Consider for example the model below. It should sample from a bivariate normal, whose mean and precision are constructed from two other distributions. I define an unnormalized density "dmymnorm" for the bivariate normal and assign to it an AF_slice sampler. Yet, upon running MCMC I get the error that "rmymnorm" is not defined. But I don't think the AF_slice sampler needs it. I don't quite understand why this code doesn't work, whereas my previous example (pasted again below, slightly modified) did. Can you give me any insights? Thank you very much!

Cheers,
Luca


############################################################
#### Code that doesn't work:

library('nimble')

dmymnorm <- nimbleFunction(

run = function(x=double(1), mean=double(1), prec=double(2), log=integer(0, default=0)){
lp <- -sum(asRow(x-mean) %*% prec %*% asCol(x-mean))/2
if(log) return(lp)
else return(exp(lp))
returnType(double(0))

})
assign('dmymnorm', dmymnorm, envir=.GlobalEnv)

code <- nimbleCode({
mean ~ dnorm(mean=0, sd=1)
sd ~ dgamma(shape=2, rate=1)

means[1:2] <- c(mean, mean)
prec[1:2,1:2] <- diag(c(1/sd^2, 1/(sd/10)^2))

x[1:2] ~ dmymnorm(mean=means[1:2], prec=prec[1:2,1:2])
})

constants <- list()
inits <- list(mean=0, sd=1)
modeldata <- list()

model <- nimbleModel(code=code, name='model', constants=constants, inits=inits, data=modeldata)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model, showCompilerOutput = TRUE, resetFunctions = TRUE)

confmodel <- configureMCMC(Cmodel)
confmodel$addSampler(target='x', type='AF_slice', control=list(sliceAdaptFactorMaxIter=1000, sliceAdaptFactorInterval=100, sliceAdaptWidthMaxIter=500, sliceMaxSteps=100, maxContractions=100))

confmodel$addMonitors('x')

confmodel
## ===== Monitors =====
## thin = 1: mean, sd, x
## ===== Samplers =====
## posterior_predictive_branch sampler (2)
## - mean
## - sd
## AF_slice sampler (1)
## - x

mcmc <- buildMCMC(confmodel)

samples <- runMCMC(mcmc=mcmc, niter=2000, nburnin=1000, inits=list(x=0:1))
## Warning: running an uncompiled MCMC algorithm, use compileNimble() for faster execution.
## running chain 1...
## Error: user-defined distribution dmymnorm provided without random generation function



############################################################
#### Code that works:
##
code2 <- nimbleCode({
means[1:2] <- c(0, 1)
prec[1:2,1:2] <- diag(c(1, 0.1))
##
x[1:2] ~ dmymnorm(mean=means[1:2], prec=prec[1:2,1:2])
})

constants <- list()
inits <- list(x=0:1)
modeldata <- list()

model2 <- nimbleModel(code=code2, name='model2', constants=constants, inits=inits, data=modeldata)
Cmodel2 <- compileNimble(model2, showCompilerOutput = TRUE, resetFunctions = TRUE)

confmodel2 <- configureMCMC(Cmodel2, nodes=NULL)
confmodel2$addSampler(target='x', type='AF_slice', control=list(sliceAdaptFactorMaxIter=1000, sliceAdaptFactorInterval=100, sliceAdaptWidthMaxIter=500, sliceMaxSteps=100, maxContractions=100))
confmodel2$addMonitors('x')

confmodel2
## ===== Monitors =====
## thin = 1: x
## ===== Samplers =====
## AF_slice sampler (1)
## - x

mcmc2 <- buildMCMC(confmodel2)
samples2 <- runMCMC(mcmc=mcmc2,niter=2000,nburnin=1000,inits=list(x=0:1))
## ...Yields correct-looking samples

Luca, can you try just providing an initial value for the bivariate node x[1:2] ?  For example:

inits <- list(mean=0, sd=1, x=c(0,0))

I think the MCMC is just trying to initialize the model at the onset (since they're no initial value provided for x), so it's trying to call the "rmymnorm" function, which doesn't exist.  I think supplying any valid initial value for x will get you going.

Daniel

parts: Hi Daniel, thank you for looking into this!
> Luca, can you try just providing an initial value for the bivariate node x[1:2] ?

I tried providing initial values for x (in nimbleModel, or in runMCMC, or both), but I still got the same error.

However, changing the sampler for the parent variables to "posterior_predictive" (as opposed to the default "posterior_predictive_branch") AND giving initial values for x did work! I paste below a simplified code that's working. So it seems that the "..._branch" sampler doesn't work well with child nodes lacking rDist-like samplers. I tried also the slice sampler for the parent variables, and that works too.

To be honest I haven't quite understood the "posterior_predictive" and "posterior_predictive_branch" samplers and their difference. I assume the first draws from "rDist", and the second is apparently doing something different.

Regarding the necessity of initial values, I've noticed that the $run() method doesn't accept any, but runMCMC() does. So is the latter recommended for the initial run at least?


Of course in my example it doesn't really make sense to use a separate Markov-Chain sampler for the child nodes, as it would be trying to explore a log-probability that is not fixed. But I wanted to see if that was possible in principle. I'm really amazed by Nimble's versatility and power!

Thank you all again! (I'll soon post some questions about model rewriting and parallelization)


#### Working code:

library('nimble')

dmymnorm <- nimbleFunction(
run = function(x=double(1), mean=double(1), prec=double(2), log=integer(0, default=0)){
lp <- -sum(asRow(x-mean) %*% prec %*% asCol(x-mean))/2
if(log) return(lp)
else return(exp(lp))
returnType(double(0))
})
assign('dmymnorm',dmymnorm,envir=.GlobalEnv)

code <- nimbleCode({
mean ~ dgamma(shape=2, rate=2) ## just to make sure to avoid conjugacy
means[1:2] <- c(mean, mean)

x[1:2] ~ dmymnorm(mean=means[1:2], prec=prec[1:2,1:2])
})

constants <- list()
inits <- list()

modeldata <- list()

model <- nimbleModel(code=code, name='model', constants=constants, inits=inits, data=modeldata)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model, showCompilerOutput = TRUE, resetFunctions = TRUE)

## Does not work with the default sampler for 'mean'
confmodel <- configureMCMC(Cmodel, nodes=NULL)
confmodel$addSampler(target=c('mean'), type='posterior_predictive', control=list())
confmodel$addSampler(target='x', type='AF_slice', control=list(sliceAdaptFactorMaxIter=5000, sliceAdaptFactorInterval=500, sliceAdaptWidthMaxIter=500, sliceMaxSteps=100, maxContractions=100))
confmodel$setMonitors(c('mean','x','logProb_x'))

confmodel
## ===== Monitors =====

## thin = 1: mean, x, logProb_x
## ===== Samplers =====
## posterior_predictive sampler (1)
## - mean

## AF_slice sampler (1)
## - x

##

mcmc <- buildMCMC(confmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(mcmc)

samples <- runMCMC(mcmc=Cmcmc, niter=10000, nburnin=5000, thin=5, inits=list(x=1:2))
## works, and returns the correct logProb_x

For example:
>
> inits <- list(mean=0, sd=1, x=c(0,0))

Luca, these are good questions.  Let me try to answer some of them.  And big thanks for the kind words about the flexibility of NIMBLE.

About the posterior_predictive (hereafter "pp") and the posterior_predictive_branch ("ppb") samplers - and the difference - and the insightful problem that you ran into.  The pp sampler is written to sample *single* trailing *non-data* stochastic nodes, which "hang off" the bottom of a (downward oriented) directed graph (representation of the hierarchical model).  For example, if:

theta ~ dSomething()
y ~ dSomething2(theta)   ## y is data
z ~ dSomething3(y)

then z is a *single* non-data stochastic node, which would be assigned a pp sampler.  And yes, you're right, that's exactly what the pp sampler does, it generates samples by taking a draw from the corresponding "r" function.

This highlights an important caveat in the pp sampler, which I'm not sure we deal with at the moment.  For any nodes assigned a pp sampler, NIMBLE ought to ensure that a proper "rSomething" generation function actually exists.

Related, the ppb sampler is designed for non-data stochastic nodes which are "branch points" for arbitrary networks of other (exclusively) non-data stochastic nodes.  Continuing the previous example:

theta ~ dSomething()
y ~ dSomething2(theta)   ## y is data
z ~ dSomething3(y)
for(i in 1:5)
      w[i] ~ dSomething4(z)
v ~ dSomething5(w[4])

Here, z is a "branch point", after which a network of exclusively non-data stochastic nodes follow.  So here, a ppb sampler would be assigned to z. The ppb sampler makes a single call to the "r" generation functions of the entire branch of stochastic nodes.  This is beneficial over assigning individual pp samplers to each node in the "branch" for the purposes of MCMC mixing, where updates to other nodes in the model would be hindered by the one-at-a-time updates to the branch nodes - in particular, by the slow resulting mixing of the branch node itself (here, z).

Again, this raises the requirement that all nodes in these trailing predictive "branches" have a valid "r" generation function, something which is not currently checked or enforced.  So, your observations and comments are helpful for the improved development of NIMBLE.

This also raises the caution that in your model assigning *only* pp samplers to mean and sd, but no sampler to x, would never update the value of x.  It would remain at whatever initial value was provided for x, and essentially be treated as "data" even though it wasn't specified as data.  Worse yet, the "pp" samplers operating on mean and sd would disregard the presence of x, and merely sample both mean and sd from their priors.  So that approach does not seem appropriate.

Finally, regarding mcmc$run(...) versus runMCMC(mcmc, ...).  The mcmc$run(...) method is in fact the core MCMC algorithm.  Originally, that was the only way to run the MCMC.  And internally, that's exactly what runMCMC(mcmc, ...) is eventually doing: calling the mcmc$run(...).  Later, the runMCMC(mcmc, ...) function was added to NIMBLE as a convenience, and it's developed into the main way users interact with the MCMC.  It provides a number of conveniences, for example easy access to WAIC, summary statistics, running multiple chains, and setting initial values.  So you're fine using either mechanism for calling the MCMC.  Providing initial values to runMCMC() - for a single chain - is equivalent to setting the initial values directly into the (compiled) model object, e.g.

Cmodel$mean <- 3   ## initialValueForMean

then executing the mcmc using mcmc$run(...).  And for multiple chains, one would have to make multiple calls to mcmc$run(...), setting initial values between each.

I hope this clears up some of your questions.  And we'll take a careful look at the checks and requirements for assignment of the pp and ppb samplers.

Cheers,
Daniel

         returnType(double(0))

})

samples <- runMCMC(mcmc=Cmcmc, niter=10000, nburnin=5000, thin=5, inits=list(x=1:2))
## works, and returns the correct logProb_x

> then z is a *single* non-data stochastic node, which would be assigned a pp sampler.  And yes, you're right, that's exactly what the pp sampler does, it generates samples by taking a draw from the corresponding "r" function.
>
> This highlights an important caveat in the pp sampler, which I'm not sure we deal with at the moment.  For any nodes assigned a pp sampler, NIMBLE ought to ensure that a proper "rSomething" generation function actually exists.
>
> Related, the ppb sampler is designed for non-data stochastic nodes which are "branch points" for arbitrary networks of other (exclusively) non-data stochastic nodes.  Continuing the previous example:
>
> theta ~ dSomething()
> y ~ dSomething2(theta)   ## y is data
> z ~ dSomething3(y)
> for(i in 1:5)
>       w[i] ~ dSomething4(z)
> v ~ dSomething5(w[4])
>
> Here, z is a "branch point", after which a network of exclusively non-data stochastic nodes follow.  So here, a ppb sampler would be assigned to z. The ppb sampler makes a single call to the "r" generation functions of the entire branch of stochastic nodes.  This is beneficial over assigning individual pp samplers to each node in the "branch" for the purposes of MCMC mixing, where updates to other nodes in the model would be hindered by the one-at-a-time updates to the branch nodes - in particular, by the slow resulting mixing of the branch node itself (here, z).
>
> Again, this raises the requirement that all nodes in these trailing predictive "branches" have a valid "r" generation function, something which is not currently checked or enforced.  So, your observations and comments are helpful for the improved development of NIMBLE.
>
> This also raises the caution that in your model assigning *only* pp samplers to mean and sd, but no sampler to x, would never update the value of x.  It would remain at whatever initial value was provided for x, and essentially be treated as "data" even though it wasn't specified as data.  Worse yet, the "pp" samplers operating on mean and sd would disregard the presence of x, and merely sample both mean and sd from their priors.  So that approach does not seem appropriate.
>
> Finally, regarding mcmc$run(...) versus runMCMC(mcmc, ...).  The mcmc$run(...) method is in fact the core MCMC algorithm.  Originally, that was the only way to run the MCMC.  And internally, that's exactly what runMCMC(mcmc, ...) is eventually doing: calling the mcmc$run(...).  Later, the runMCMC(mcmc, ...) function was added to NIMBLE as a convenience, and it's developed into the main way users interact with the MCMC.  It provides a number of conveniences, for example easy access to WAIC, summary statistics, running multiple chains, and setting initial values.  So you're fine using either mechanism for calling the MCMC.  Providing initial values to runMCMC() - for a single chain - is equivalent to setting the initial values directly into the (compiled) model object, e.g.
>
> Cmodel$mean <- 3   ## initialValueForMean
>
> then executing the mcmc using mcmc$run(...).  And for multiple chains, one would have to make multiple calls to mcmc$run(...), setting initial values between each.
